newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Adecco sales up, France lags.
newsitem.headline: Adecco sales up, France lags.

text.p: Europe's largest temporary employment concern, Adecco SA, said Tuesday that its sales rose 5.2 percent in the first nine months of 1996, but business was hobbled by the weak European economy.

"Against the background of the difficult economic siutation in France, Germany and Switzerland, we are very satisfied with Adecco's increased turnover," said John Bowmer, Adecco's chief executive officer, in a statement.
Adecco, formed by a merger of Swiss temporary employment firm Adia SA and French part-time employment firm Ecco SA earlier this year, and rivals U.S. market-leader Manpower Inc in size.

In its first published business results since the merger, Adecco said it would not release earnings figures until the merger was finalised "on a book-keeping basis." It was also waiting until Ecco has been valued according to U.S. generally accepted accounting principle guidelines.

But it did publish joint revenues, which totaled 6.306 billion Swiss francs in the first nine months, compared with 5.996 billion calculated for 1995. The figures excluded results from the security and cleaning businesses, which were sold.
Sales for the third quarter alone showed a rise of 6.7 percent to 2.356 billion Swiss francs compared with the comparable 1995 quarter when calculated on the same basis as nine-month sales.
Sales for the third quarter from ordinary activities only totaled 2.024 billion Swiss francs.

Adecco said that if acquisitions of U.K. firm Roevin, U.S. firm Big Company Inc (BCI), and sale of Personnel Group of America (PGA) were omitted from results, third-quarter sales would show a rise of 8.6 percent and nine-month sales a rise of 7.8 percent.

Business remained slack in the single largest market of France, where sales for the first nine months fell 3.4 percent to 2.854 billion Swiss francs, from 2.940 billion in the 1995 period. Sales were also down four percent in the third quarter alone, at 1.061 billion versus 1.104 billion. No significant improvement is expected this year.
But business elsewhere in Europe developed "quite satisfactorily," Adecco said.
The dollar's rise in the third quarter versus the Swiss franc also had a positive impact on turnover.
A 20 percent drop in the value of the yen reduced the results significantly in Swiss francs from Asia, however.
CS Research analyst Christoph Gretler said it was difficult to estimate results because the two separate concerns have very different business activities.
He now expectes the combined earnings for all of 1996 at 265 million Swiss francs, a slight reduction from his earlier forecasts of 275 million.
He said the 7.8 percent growth in turnover was higher than expected. But the weakness in France was worrisome.
"The problem is the European economic situation," he said.
